q: A motor yacht is keeping pace with you, as shown. How do you tell the skipper where it is?
why: Abeam is at right angles to the boat; starboard is the right-hand side, facing forward.

q: Snorkelling under the boat at anchor, you find a plastic bag wrapped round the blade right aft, just behind the propeller. What is it caught on?
why: The rudder is the steering blade at the stern, just behind the propeller.

q: A guest from the next boat asks if they may use your heads. Where do you take them?
why: On a boat the toilet is called the heads.

q: After a bumpy crossing the skipper asks you to check the bilge. Where do you look?
a: Under the saloon floorboards, at the lowest point
o: In the cockpit lockers under the seats
In the anchor locker at the bow
In the fresh-water tank under a berth
why: The bilge is the lowest part inside the hull, where any water collects.

q: The skipper asks you where the wind is coming from, relative to the boat. What do you answer?
why: The quarter lies between abeam and astern; here the wind comes from aft on the right-hand side.

q: You have just cleared into Turkey and the skipper hands you the Turkish courtesy flag. Where do you hoist it?
o: At the top of the forestay
why: A courtesy flag flies under the starboard spreader; the stern is for your own ensign.

q: Entering a shallow bay, the skipper asks you to watch the depth sounder. Which figure tells you how much depth the boat needs?
why: Draft is how far the keel reaches below the waterline.

q: The marina office asks for the boat's size to find you a berth between two other yachts. Which two figures do they need?
why: A berth between boats must fit the overall length and the width (beam).

q: Waves are starting to slop into the cockpit and the skipper asks you to put the washboards in. Which opening do they close?
o: The anchor locker at the bow
The forward hatch over the berth
why: Washboards slot into the companionway so water in the cockpit cannot pour below.

q: Before a windy crossing, the skipper asks you to check the wires that hold the mast up from the sides for broken strands. Which do you check?
why: Shrouds support the mast sideways; the forestay and backstay hold it fore and aft.

q: Motoring slowly into a sandy bay, you feel a soft bump from below and the boat stops. Which part has most likely touched the bottom?
why: The keel is the deepest part of the boat; draft is measured to its bottom.

q: The skipper says: "We'll anchor in the lee of the island tonight." Which spot does she mean?
o: A or C, whichever is closer
why: The lee is the side sheltered from the wind: with a north wind, the south side.

fig.note: Wind N 20 kn, sea from the north

q: You come back in the tender. The yacht's sides are high, and it has a low bathing platform at the stern. Where do you climb aboard?
a: At the stern, where the freeboard is lowest
o: At the bow, holding on to the forestay
Amidships, over the top of the guardrail
At the bow, up the anchor chain
why: Freeboard is the height of the deck above the water; board where it is lowest.

q: As you approach the berth, the skipper calls: "Two crew aft, please!" Where do you go?
why: Aft means towards the stern; forward means towards the bow.

q: You come on deck at night and see the boom eased out over the starboard side. Which side is windward?
a: Port: the boom goes out to leeward
o: Starboard: the boom points into the wind
Starboard: the side the boat heels to
You cannot tell without a compass
why: The wind pushes the boom away from it, so the boom is always on the leeward side.

q: You are helping to unfurl the genoa. Which wire is the sail rolled round?
a: The forestay, from the bow up the mast
o: The backstay, from the stern up the mast
A shroud, from the side deck up the mast
The main halyard, inside the mast
why: A roller-furling genoa rolls up round the forestay at the bow.

q: The skipper asks how much water there is under the keel. What do you answer?
why: 2.6 m below the waterline minus 2.1 m of draft leaves 0.5 m under the keel.

fig.title: Depth sounder
lines: Set to show depth below the waterline

q: With the wind as shown, the skipper asks you to sit on the windward side, and later to tip a bucket of washing-up water over the side. Which sides do you use?
a: Sit to starboard; tip the bucket to port
o: Sit to port; tip the bucket to starboard
Sit to port; tip the bucket to port
Sit to starboard; tip it to starboard
why: Windward is the side the wind comes from (starboard); anything thrown out goes to leeward.

q: You spot this while going forward. What do you do?
a: Tell the skipper before the tack: it takes the load then
o: Nothing: that shroud is slack, so it is safe
Mention it in harbour this evening
Wait for the tack, then take a closer look
why: After the tack the starboard shroud is to windward and holds the mast up; a loose fitting can fail.

fig.title: Under way, port tack
lines: Wind 18 kn over the port side
Skipper plans to tack in 10 minutes

q: You are sitting in the cockpit facing aft, towards the stern. The skipper asks you to hang a fender on the port side. Which side is that from where you sit?
o: The side the wind comes from
why: Port and starboard belong to the boat, seen facing forward; facing aft, port is on your right.
